title: Shapes and Spatial Understanding
description: Comprehensive shared preparation notes and worked practice for Shapes and Spatial Understanding. Review the target examination syllabus and level before reuse.

coverage: Spatial reasoning through construction and visualisation

sections.label: Concepts and worked examples
sections.html:
Shape properties and classification

Classify figures using defining properties rather than appearance. A polygon is a closed plane figure made of straight segments. Quadrilaterals can be grouped by parallel sides, equal sides, right angles and symmetry; categories can overlap, such as a square being both a rectangle and a rhombus.

Three-dimensional objects

Prisms have two congruent parallel bases; pyramids have one base and triangular faces meeting at an apex. A cylinder has two circular bases and one curved surface; a cone has one circular base and an apex. Nets show faces before folding.

Transformations and scale

Translation slides, rotation turns and reflection flips a figure. These rigid transformations preserve lengths and angles. Similar figures have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides; congruent figures are the same shape and size.

Worked example: A rectangle with side lengths 3 cm and 5 cm has area 15 cm^2 and perimeter 16 cm. A scale factor of 2 makes corresponding lengths 6 cm and 10 cm, perimeter 32 cm, and area 60 cm^2.

sections.label: Methods and exam checks
sections.html:
• Ask which property defines a class and which properties are only typical examples.
  • Use a fold, tracing or dynamic diagram to test symmetry and congruence.
  • Distinguish a prism's two matching bases from its lateral faces.
  • Use the same orientation and units when comparing corresponding sides.
  • Let learners build, draw, describe and then formalise a shape relationship.

sections.label: Key facts and formulas
sections.html:
• A rectangle has four right angles; a rhombus has four equal sides; a square has both sets of properties.
  • Congruent figures have equal corresponding lengths and angles.
  • Similar figures preserve angle measures and use one scale factor for all corresponding lengths.
  • Euler's relation for a convex polyhedron is (\(V-E+F=2\)).

sections.label: Worked practice
sections.html:
1. Core:

    How many sides does a hexagon have?

    1. (\(5\))
    2. (\(6\))
    3. (\(7\))
    4. (\(8\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(6\))

    The prefix “hexa-” indicates six; a hexagon has six sides.

  2. Core:

    How many faces does a rectangular prism have?

    1. (\(4\))
    2. (\(5\))
    3. (\(6\))
    4. (\(8\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(6\))

    A rectangular prism has top, bottom, front, back, left and right faces: six in total.

  3. Foundation:

    Which property is shared by every rectangle?

    1. All four sides are equal
    2. Opposite sides are equal and all angles are right angles
    3. Exactly one pair of parallel sides
    4. No parallel sides
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: Opposite sides are equal and all angles are right angles

    A rectangle has two pairs of equal opposite sides and four right angles.

  4. Standard:

    A similar triangle has a side corresponding to 6 cm on a 4 cm side. What is the scale factor from the first triangle to the second?

    1. (\(2/3\))
    2. (\(3/2\))
    3. (\(2\))
    4. (\(10\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(3/2\))

    Scale factor is corresponding new length divided by original: (\(6/4=3/2\)).

  5. Challenge:

    A convex polyhedron has 8 vertices and 12 edges. How many faces does it have?

    1. (\(4\))
    2. (\(6\))
    3. (\(8\))
    4. (\(12\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(6\))

    Euler's relation is (\(V-E+F=2\)). Thus (\(8-12+F=2\)), so (\(F=6\)).
